title: How does JPA/Spring Data auditing with @CreatedDate and @LastModifiedDate differ from Hibernate Envers @Audited history tables?
keyPoints: @CreatedDate and @LastModifiedDate stamp when the current row was created and last changed.
@CreatedBy and @LastModifiedBy stamp who changed it, requiring an AuditorAware bean for the current user.
@EnableJpaAuditing on a configuration class activates the Spring Data auditing mechanism.
Spring Data auditing tracks only the latest state on the current row: old values are overwritten.
Hibernate Envers @Audited maintains full revision history in separate audit tables (entity_AUD + REVINFO).
Envers allows querying any past state of an entity using AuditReader and revision numbers.
Use both together: Spring Data auditing for cheap current-row stamps, Envers for compliance history trails.

s1_definition.oneliner: @CreatedDate and @LastModifiedDate stamp when the current row was last touched, while Hibernate Envers @Audited maintains full version history in separate audit tables for every change.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **@CreatedDate** -- automatically sets the creation timestamp when an entity is first persisted.
- **@LastModifiedDate** -- automatically updates the modification timestamp on every save.
- **@CreatedBy / @LastModifiedBy** -- automatically sets who created or last modified the entity, pulling the username from an `AuditorAware` bean.
- **@EnableJpaAuditing** -- Spring Boot annotation that activates the auditing mechanism.
- **@EntityListeners(AuditingEntityListener.class)** -- registers the listener that fills the auditing fields.
- **Hibernate Envers @Audited** -- maintains full revision history by writing every version of an entity to separate audit tables.
- **AuditReader** -- Envers API for querying historical revisions of an entity.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, Spring Data auditing is like writing "last updated by Priya on 23-Oct, created by Rajesh on 1-Jan" in the margin of the current passbook page. You see who last touched it and when, but not the history of changes. Hibernate Envers is like keeping a photocopy of the passbook every single time anything changes, filed in a separate archive room. With Envers you can pull up exactly what Rajesh's balance was on any date in the past and who changed it.

sections.s6_takeaway:
There are two layers of auditing in JPA and they answer different questions. Spring Data auditing uses @CreatedDate, @LastModifiedDate, @CreatedBy, and @LastModifiedBy with an AuditingEntityListener to stamp when and who on the current row. It is cheap, adds only four columns, and answers "when was this last touched and by whom." But it overwrites old values, so you cannot see what the balance was before the latest change.

Hibernate Envers is a different tool for a different need. By adding the @Audited annotation and the hibernate-envers dependency, Hibernate maintains full revision history in separate audit tables. Every insert, update, and delete writes a revision row, so you can use AuditReader to reconstruct exactly what an entity looked like at any past revision. The cost is higher because every change writes an extra row, and audit tables grow forever.

In our National Bank of India system, both are used together. The current account row carries created and updated stamps so support staff can see at a glance when it last changed. Envers keeps the compliance history so that when a regulator asks what Rajesh's balance was on March 15 and who changed it, we can answer precisely. Banking regulations frequently mandate seven-year audit trails, and current-row stamps cannot satisfy that because old values are overwritten.

Remember one sentence: Spring Data auditing stamps when and who on the current row for convenience, while Envers @Audited preserves every historical version in separate audit tables for compliance and forensic queries.
